title: Introduction to Generative AI & Why Lawyers Should Care — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source provides a complementary rationale for legal AI—law is language-based, standardized and supported by trusted legal and organizational materials—but does not assess the cluster’s central claims about expert-designed agentic workflows, tacit knowledge-transfer difficulties, evaluation or retained human checkpoints.
qs: And then in our organizations, if you’re thinking about a law firm, your internal document management system; if you’re in a court, the opinions of the judges that sit on your court.
Those combinations of it being a language-based industry with a language-based machine, our templatized writing, and our trustworthy underlying sources—it’s sort of a recipe for impact on what we do.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The source only introduces an ongoing exploration of AI’s effects on law and establishes McCormack’s dispute-resolution credentials. It does not take a substantive position on AI assistance versus machine adjudication, process redesign, safeguards, access, or the evidentiary basis for efficiency and reliability claims.
qs: We’re really excited to convene a conversation between the two of us on a regular basis to talk all about how we perceive the future of law to be impacted by AI as it unfolds in real time.

Right now I’m the CEO and President at the American Arbitration Association, which is the largest provider of ADR services in the world—we administered over half a million cases last year outside of courts.

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: The source supports the descriptive claim that generative AI differs from familiar AI by producing new content through token prediction. However, it does not address the cluster’s central requirement that lawyers or judicial officers verify, supervise and remain responsible for generated legal work, nor does it evaluate legal-task performance or reliability.
qs: The difference is that in 2017, a team at Google encountered a breakthrough in artificial intelligence when they started using what was called a transformer architecture, which, as I understand it, is essentially predicting the next most likely word—or in AI parlance, token—in a series of words or tokens to produce new content in response to prompts from human beings.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: The source accepts the need for broad curricular adaptation and adds a concrete AI-enabled mechanism: customized GPTs for real-time formative feedback. It also links technology, design thinking, professionalism and client focus, while presenting benefits as prospective rather than measured.
qs: And I think that creates real opportunities for schools that have been building a muscle for a while at integrating technology, design thinking, systems redesign, professionalism and client focus, to emerge as real leaders in the employment market.

So I’m excited at the idea that we can put into the hands of students their own ability to create customized GPTs that are trained on their professors’ sample exams, outlines from upper-class students, hornbooks, those kinds of things, and test against that in real time to figure out if they’re actually learning what they need to be learning.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: junior rote work currently develops judgment, strategy and client-service capability, and AI-driven compression of that work threatens associate development and the future leadership pipeline. It anticipates institutional rethinking and ongoing education, but does not materially extend the cluster’s proposed replacement model of simulation, mentorship and independent practice.
qs: And the last reason is that we have an apprenticeship-based model of lawyer formation in the early years, where we spend a long time doing rote tasks in isolation from the broader representation, and those become the building blocks of judgment and strategy and client service.

In a world where that time period collapses—where the tasks that make up that work go away or are changed—that has enormous implications for what your junior lawyers are doing, how your in-house talent teams are able to support them, and what the future leadership of your firm looks like.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source supports continuous learning through accessible technology discussions and encourages lawyers to engage with generative AI rather than assume they are irretrievably behind. Its evidence is experiential and anecdotal, consistent with the cluster’s caution that professional conversations provide contextual awareness without independently validating broader adoption or learning outcomes. It does not materially develop the cluster’s stronger emphasis on filtering information rather than chasing releases.
qs: And so the combination of our risk aversion and then not really being privy to the conversations about what’s changing creates an opportunity, I think, to advance that conversation and make sure we are staying current.
And so I hope that’s one of the things people take away: I think anybody can get caught up and roll up their sleeves and get involved.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central framing: court AI should be evaluated against severe existing access-to-justice failures rather than an idealised human system. It identifies widespread lack of affordable representation, points to court chatbots for self-represented litigants as a practical starting point, and couples optimism with critical judgment and safe deployment. Its claims illustrate opportunity rather than demonstrate improved outcomes, consistent with the synthesis’s evidentiary caution.
qs: The civil justice system in America is basically a massive market failure in that 92% of Americans can’t afford help to navigate their civil justice problems.
And I would say that’s our shared worldview, recognizing that there needs to be critical thought applied and safe deployment.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by treating AI as a significant pressure on law-firm pricing, leveraged labour, client service and lawyer development, while expecting hourly billing to persist within a mixed pricing portfolio. It also supports buyer-led redesign, arguing that in-house departments can restructure operations and redirect spending, though its claims are primarily prospective and do not address verification in depth.
qs: Jen Leonard: I think law firm leaders should care deeply, mainly because of how their business is structured and the way they serve clients, the way they generate revenue, the way that they train and develop new lawyers.
I’m not betting against it; I think it will always remain part of a pricing portfolio.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s access-oriented proposition by identifying extensive unmet civil legal need and presenting court-provided chatbots as scalable assistance for self-represented litigants. Its support is optimistic and largely prospective: it reports one deployment but provides no measured outcomes and does not address verification, reliability, remedy, inequality or risk-shifting concerns.
qs: The civil justice system in America is basically a massive market failure in that 92% of Americans can’t afford help to navigate their civil justice problems.

There’s actually at least one court—maybe there are more, but there’s one that I’m aware of in Maricopa County, Arizona, where the court’s creative coordinator has built his own custom GPTs (again, based on the technology that OpenAI has—the GPT framework) to produce chatbots to help self-represented parties with different legal problems.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that AI may weaken the coupled law-firm model of junior-generated revenue, leverage and apprenticeship. It also supports the cluster’s buyer-side mechanism by predicting that in-house teams could absorb overflow work while continuing to use firms for specialist advice. Its claims are qualitative and conditional, consistent with the synthesis’s caution that structural change is not yet established.
qs: But that leveraged labor model will continue to be under pressure as the technology becomes more capable of doing some of the tasks that junior associates currently bill for, which contribute in a massive way to the revenue that law firms generate.

In a world where that time period collapses—where the tasks that make up that work go away or are changed—that has enormous implications for what your junior lawyers are doing, how your in-house talent teams are able to support them, and what the future leadership of your firm looks like.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by treating generative AI as a structural business-model issue rather than merely a productivity tool. It specifically reinforces pressure on associate leverage, buyer-led insourcing of overflow work, and disruption to apprenticeship-based lawyer development. Its claims are conditional predictions and do not address the cluster’s broader points on pricing, provider convergence, governance or capital structures.
qs: But that leveraged labor model will continue to be under pressure as the technology becomes more capable of doing some of the tasks that junior associates currently bill for, which contribute in a massive way to the revenue that law firms generate.

That second bucket could be absorbed by technology in-house, which would make the GC look really great to their C-suite if they’re able to spend their legal dollars on the more high-end, business strategy questions that the business wants to solve.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of generative AI’s relevance to language-intensive legal work and the value of legal-specific and organisation-specific context layered over general foundation models. It does not materially address lawyer–engineer collaboration, workflow integration or the verified-copilot model, so its support is narrower than the full synthesis.
qs: Those combinations of it being a language-based industry with a language-based machine, our templatized writing, and our trustworthy underlying sources—it’s sort of a recipe for impact on what we do.

Jen Leonard: Yeah, so my understanding of the technology is if you hear people talking about, you know, a certain law firm or organization building a model in-house, what that really means is they are building on top of one of these foundational models from one of the major tech companies.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: Leonard and McCormack align with the cluster’s core view that generative AI could improve public legal service and access to justice, while treating those benefits as opportunities rather than demonstrated outcomes. Their insistence on critical thought and safe deployment also supports the distinction between technological uptake and meaningful service transformation.
qs: Some of what I have viewed as the biggest problems in the legal profession and the way it serves our neighbors—our communities—feel like they could be really impacted positively by this new technology.
And I would say that’s our shared worldview, recognizing that there needs to be critical thought applied and safe deployment.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source directly endorses practitioner engagement, continuing education and experimentation rather than waiting for certainty. It also treats access to justice as a potential benefit while expressly requiring critical thought and safe deployment; its claims are predominantly experience-based and predictive, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caveats.
qs: And so I hope that’s one of the things people take away: I think anybody can get caught up and roll up their sleeves and get involved.
And I would say that’s our shared worldview, recognizing that there needs to be critical thought applied and safe deployment.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI’s legal value depends on institutional and business-model change rather than research or drafting capability alone. It anticipates redesign of firm revenue, staffing, training, in-house operations, education, courts and regulation, while treating many resulting efficiencies and structural effects as predictions rather than measured outcomes. It gives less attention to verification and task-level evaluation than the cluster does, but does not conflict with them.
qs: Jen Leonard: I think law firm leaders should care deeply, mainly because of how their business is structured and the way they serve clients, the way they generate revenue, the way that they train and develop new lawyers.

They can rethink what their ops teams can do and how they do it, and therefore where they can put their dollars on those trickier, harder, bigger questions where they might not have the expertise on their team because it’s not something they need day to day.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source directly endorses engagement rather than waiting for certainty: it encourages lawyers to catch up, participate and use continuing education and practical resources to navigate generative AI. Its hoped-for benefits to professional well-being and client service are explicitly prospective, consistent with the cluster’s distinction between an action agenda and demonstrated outcomes.
qs: And so I hope that’s one of the things people take away: I think anybody can get caught up and roll up their sleeves and get involved.
Like you said, we’re going to work on some other materials, courses, opportunities to help lawyers who are trying to think about the best way forward and through all of this.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central move beyond narrow model-output performance toward AI’s implications for legal-service delivery and unmet civil legal need. However, it provides no concrete implementation, verification or task-specific evaluation framework, so it does not materially extend the cluster’s reliable-delivery account.
qs: We look through this tiny lens at our research products in legal and they’re, you know, hallucinating at X rate and “this certainly is the end of it.” But this is a much, much bigger rollout and deployment across all organizations and individual consumers.
The civil justice system in America is basically a massive market failure in that 92% of Americans can’t afford help to navigate their civil justice problems.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source endorses AI as an augmentative tool for lawyers and legal departments, particularly as a strategy thought partner and a means of gaining workflow insight. This aligns with selective augmentation, though it does not address the cluster’s central constraints of verification, retained responsibility or uneven empirical gains.
qs: I have found it very helpful as a thought partner for strategy development.

Bridget McCormack: Yeah, I mean, I know some general counsels’ departments that are doing things with their billing using the technology, and it’s allowing them to learn things about their own workflows that were just harder to know without this kind of advancement in the technology.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that AI pressures production-based law-firm economics more than it eliminates lawyers. It predicts pressure on associate leverage and hourly billing, selective insourcing by legal departments, continued demand for sophisticated outside expertise, and disruption to apprenticeship-based training. Its claims are mainly causal predictions rather than evidence of realised market-wide change, consistent with the cluster’s uncertainty caveats.
qs: But that leveraged labor model will continue to be under pressure as the technology becomes more capable of doing some of the tasks that junior associates currently bill for, which contribute in a massive way to the revenue that law firms generate.

That second bucket could be absorbed by technology in-house, which would make the GC look really great to their C-suite if they’re able to spend their legal dollars on the more high-end, business strategy questions that the business wants to solve.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Leonard and McCormack align with the cluster’s framing of legal AI as service and organisational redesign rather than a discrete software purchase. They connect adoption to workflow visibility, in-house and outside-counsel relationships, leadership, education and the incentives created by hours-based revenue, while presenting the expected benefits mainly as opportunities rather than established outcomes.
qs: You know, the same way—  If law firms get this right, they can rebuild the way they serve their clients and the kinds of value they provide their clients.
We are tethered to 24 hours in a day, and it seems like we end up working most of them because that’s our revenue model in the private sector—you have to work as many as you possibly can.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core claim that generative AI will redesign and reallocate legal work rather than produce a single wholesale-replacement outcome. It specifically anticipates restructuring in-house operations, pressure on junior-associate work and law-firm leverage, and disruption to apprenticeship, while acknowledging risks and uncertainty. Its claims are mainly forecasts and examples, however, and it does not substantively address the cluster’s stronger requirements around task-level testing, verification or continuous governance.
qs: But I think it also gives them this opportunity to think about how they structure their work in-house in ways that allow them to better serve their clients.

But that leveraged labor model will continue to be under pressure as the technology becomes more capable of doing some of the tasks that junior associates currently bill for, which contribute in a massive way to the revenue that law firms generate.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by predicting that AI will let in-house counsel absorb capacity-driven overflow work while preserving outside demand for sophisticated advice, pressure associate leverage, and disrupt apprenticeship-based lawyer development. Its claims are qualitative and conditional, and it does not substantively address workflow pricing reform, verification, governance or implementation.
qs: That second bucket could be absorbed by technology in-house, which would make the GC look really great to their C-suite if they’re able to spend their legal dollars on the more high-end, business strategy questions that the business wants to solve.

In a world where that time period collapses—where the tasks that make up that work go away or are changed—that has enormous implications for what your junior lawyers are doing, how your in-house talent teams are able to support them, and what the future leadership of your firm looks like.

kp.k: Risk aversion and limited time constrain lawyer engagement
kp.d: McCormack argues that lawyers' training encourages risk aversion and that professional conversations disproportionately emphasize AI risks rather than benefits. Leonard identifies limited time and difficulty following broader technology discussions as additional barriers. Both recommend participation and continuing education rather than treating unfamiliarity as evidence that it is too late to learn.
qs: I also think that lawyers are risk-averse by training, and that’s a good thing for lots of reasons. So they have been slow to adopt the technology.
nobody’s really behind unless they’re refusing to participate at all.
I think anybody can get caught up and roll up their sleeves and get involved.

kp.k: Generative capabilities fit law's language-intensive work
kp.d: Leonard describes the 2017 transformer breakthrough as enabling content generation, analysis, summarization and synthesis, with outputs expanding beyond text toward video and audio. Both speakers explicitly disclaim technological expertise. McCormack argues that law's reliance on words and relatively structured writing makes the technology immediately relevant; Leonard adds that legal publications and internal work product offer potentially trustworthy source material. These are explanations of potential suitability, not measured findings of legal accuracy.
qs: Everything that I’m learning, I’m learning over the last few years as well.
We work in words.
Legal opinions have a formula. We write in similar styles; regulations and statutes have a formula and they’re fairly structured.
Those combinations of it being a language-based industry with a language-based machine, our templatized writing, and our trustworthy underlying sources—it’s sort of a recipe for impact on what we do.

kp.k: Enterprise deployment builds on foundational models
kp.d: Leonard describes in-house legal AI development as building on major technology companies' foundational models rather than creating those capabilities independently. She emphasizes confidentiality, security, internal data boundaries and output assessment over time. McCormack reports that AAA uses Microsoft products and has been developing small tools to accelerate organizational learning. Their account presents their understanding of deployment, not documented security guarantees or technical evaluations.
qs: they are building on top of one of these foundational models from one of the major tech companies.
Obviously, ethics and confidentiality and security are critical for lawyers
fine-tuning it by testing it internally, looking at the outputs, assessing the quality, and benchmarking it over time.
And we’ve just been training small tools to expedite our learning.

kp.k: Commercial products offer smaller firms an adoption route
kp.d: McCormack identifies VLex and CoCounsel as commercially available options for lawyers whose firms cannot develop their own systems. She frames efficiency and client demands as possible adoption drivers. The speakers express uncertainty about CoCounsel's product integration at Thomson Reuters; the discussion does not provide comparative product performance evidence.
qs: there are a couple of large language models that are now being marketed to lawyers that are general-purpose models, like the VLex model and the CoCounsel model.

If your law firm is a smaller law firm and you’re not in a position to train your own model, but you think using the technology could bring efficiencies to your practice or your clients start demanding that you use it, there are models out there on the market that you can purchase.
As far as I know it’s still separate, but I could be wrong.

kp.k: Technology competition underpins expectations of continued AI expansion
kp.d: Leonard argues that decades of AI research, investment and competition among Microsoft, Amazon and Google make generative AI more than a passing legal-technology trend. She anticipates deployment through products customers already use and continued capability improvement, while acknowledging the need for guardrails, regulation and safe deployment. These are strategic interpretations and forecasts, not quantified investment or performance findings.
qs: I don’t think this is going anywhere. I think it will only improve. The investments will continue to grow.
the race among Microsoft, Amazon and Google to really dominate this market is based on their pre-existing relationship with millions of customers around the world.
their bet is they can infuse generative AI into everything that people are already using
recognizing that there needs to be critical thought applied and safe deployment.

kp.k: Court AI could address unmet civil legal needs
kp.d: McCormack characterizes American civil justice as a market failure, asserting that 92% of Americans cannot afford help navigating civil justice problems and that at least one party is unrepresented in 75% of civil cases in state courts. No supporting study is identified. She reports a Maricopa County, Arizona court coordinator's use of custom GPT chatbots for self-represented parties and predicts that better information and service could improve public confidence in justice; no outcomes evaluation is supplied.
qs: 92% of Americans can’t afford help to navigate their civil justice problems.
In state courts, in most cases, 75% of civil cases—at least one party—is unrepresented.

the court’s creative coordinator has built his own custom GPTs (again, based on the technology that OpenAI has—the GPT framework) to produce chatbots to help self-represented parties with different legal problems.
we might really grow public confidence in our public justice system.

kp.k: AI efficiency challenges hourly revenue without eliminating hourly pricing
kp.d: Leonard argues that time-based billing does not reward speed and is vulnerable to AI efficiency, but explicitly expects hourly billing to remain within a pricing portfolio. She recalls a Thomson Reuters report, while expressing uncertainty about its title, as showing the bottom of a 20-year decline in annual hours billed per timekeeper across all Am Law 200 firms, timekeepers and practice areas. She says rate increases sustained revenue growth and that the decline following the Great Recession never recovered. This is her account of external evidence, not a report reproduced in the transcript.
qs: I’m not betting against it; I think it will always remain part of a pricing portfolio.
It doesn’t necessarily reward you for doing something very quickly.
we’re actually at the bottom of a 20-year decline across all timekeepers in all Am Law 200 firms, in all practice areas, of the number of hours billed per timekeeper per year.
The thing that has offset that decline has been the rise in rates, so the revenue continues to grow over time

kp.k: Automating junior tasks threatens associate-based leverage
kp.d: Leonard predicts pressure on the leveraged labor model as AI performs tasks currently billed by junior associates. Her mechanism is the erosion of revenue generated through associates' work that extends partners' client-serving capacity. She does not quantify displacement, predict specific staffing ratios or identify an observed change in firm structure.
qs: Law firm partners come together to practice and they hire associates of all levels to leverage what they’re doing by generating more revenue

that leveraged labor model will continue to be under pressure as the technology becomes more capable of doing some of the tasks that junior associates currently bill for, which contribute in a massive way to the revenue that law firms generate.

kp.k: In-house AI could absorb outsourced overflow work
kp.d: Leonard distinguishes sophisticated matters requiring outside expertise from overflow matters outsourced because internal teams lack capacity. She predicts that AI could bring the second category in-house and redirect spending toward specialized business-strategy advice. Unlike earlier technologies primarily purchased by firms, she expects lawyers on both sides of the buying relationship to use these tools. This is a prospective redistribution of work, not measured insourcing.
qs: on both sides of the transaction now you will have lawyers using this technology.
there’s the overflow bucket where they do have the expertise, they just don’t have the person-power to actually do that work.
That second bucket could be absorbed by technology in-house
spend their legal dollars on the more high-end, business strategy questions that the business wants to solve.

kp.k: Legal departments could redesign operations and spending
kp.d: McCormack argues that corporate adoption elsewhere creates expectations of comparable efficiencies from legal departments. She anticipates redesigned legal operations, spending flexibility and better legal-spend forecasting. As anecdotal support, she reports knowing departments using AI for billing and workflow insight. Leonard separately describes personal experience using GPT-4 as a strategy-development thought partner, extending the discussion beyond research and drafting.
qs: why can’t the counsel’s office use the technology to produce the same kinds of efficiencies?
They can rethink what their ops teams can do and how they do it
They’re probably also going to be able to make a lot better predictions of where their legal spend is going in the future.

I know some general counsels’ departments that are doing things with their billing using the technology, and it’s allowing them to learn things about their own workflows that were just harder to know without this kind of advancement in the technology.
I have found it very helpful as a thought partner for strategy development.

kp.k: Automating apprenticeship tasks creates lawyer-formation challenges
kp.d: Leonard argues that repetitive early-career work has traditionally supplied building blocks for judgment, strategy and client service. If AI removes or compresses that work, she expects consequences for junior lawyers' activities, talent-team support and future firm leadership. She situates this predicted disruption after what she describes as COVID-related early-career skills disruption from virtual practice, without proposing a detailed replacement training model.
qs: we have an apprenticeship-based model of lawyer formation in the early years, where we spend a long time doing rote tasks in isolation from the broader representation, and those become the building blocks of judgment and strategy and client service.

In a world where that time period collapses—where the tasks that make up that work go away or are changed—that has enormous implications for what your junior lawyers are doing, how your in-house talent teams are able to support them, and what the future leadership of your firm looks like.
there was already a skills disruption in the early years of practice because we were doing everything virtually.

kp.k: Curricular adaptation could reshape law-school recruitment
kp.d: Leonard predicts that employers will scrutinize curricula for changing skills needs rather than relying on historically uniform legal education and established hiring relationships. She highlights opportunities for schools integrating technology, design thinking, systems redesign, professionalism and client focus, naming Suffolk and Vanderbilt as programs she and McCormack favor. McCormack agrees that innovation could open new recruiting relationships. Leonard also forecasts competition for educators able to translate practice developments into curricula and reports already seeing talent competition in firms.
qs: employers, for the first time, will have to look under the hood of different schools’ curricula to see which schools are actually adapting their curricula to respond to changing skills needs.
schools that have been building a muscle for a while at integrating technology, design thinking, systems redesign, professionalism and client focus
they can market their students to law firms that might not have spent a lot of time there before.

I think there will be a talent crisis in all organizations—and maybe law schools specifically—in finding people who are connected to the market, to the practice, to what people will be doing and have the ability to translate that into curricula and teach it with impact

kp.k: Customized tutoring could improve formative feedback
kp.d: Leonard proposes student-created custom GPTs using professors' sample exams, upper-class outlines and hornbooks to test understanding throughout a course rather than waiting for final-exam grades. She anticipates learning, well-being, diversity and inclusion benefits. McCormack supports individualized tutoring, particularly for students reluctant to disclose confusion, drawing on her own experience. These are proposed educational benefits, not results from an evaluated intervention.
qs: the lack of formative feedback that’s customized for new law students.

their own ability to create customized GPTs that are trained on their professors’ sample exams, outlines from upper-class students, hornbooks, those kinds of things, and test against that in real time to figure out if they’re actually learning what they need to be learning.
I think there are well-being benefits, there are diversity and inclusion benefits, and there are just straight-up learning benefits that can come from that.
I love the opportunity for individual feedback and tutoring, especially in a setting where some law students will have a very hard time saying it’s hard for them to understand what’s going on.

kp.k: Consumer AI challenges traditional unauthorized-practice regulation
kp.d: Leonard frames widely accessible AI as a coming enforcement challenge for state supreme courts and a potential access-to-justice resource. McCormack reports seeing coverage of a new New Jersey unauthorized-practice lawsuit against LegalZoom but cannot recall which publication carried it. She predicts that accessible custom GPTs and improving general tools will overwhelm traditional regulatory approaches, and recommends ambitious experimentation with services for people needing help. She explicitly says she lacks definitive answers; no legal holding or specific rule amendment is offered.
qs: there’s a new lawsuit against LegalZoom for the unlicensed practice of law in New Jersey.
That seems like it’s going to be very hard to keep track of in an era where you can build your own GPT even on accurate legal information.
I don’t know how the technology this time doesn’t run over the regulators.
I think I would want to take a very ambitious approach to letting some flowers grow and seeing what might happen that could help the people that need help.
I don’t have answers for them.

kp.k: Less time-dependent value could improve lawyer well-being
kp.d: Leonard envisions potential well-being benefits for experienced lawyers if AI enables firms to move away from revenue tied tightly to hours worked and toward solving client problems. This is an aspirational business-model outcome, not evidence of reduced working hours or adoption of a particular alternative fee arrangement.
qs: I’m excited about some of the well-being benefits for experienced lawyers
We are tethered to 24 hours in a day, and it seems like we end up working most of them because that’s our revenue model in the private sector—you have to work as many as you possibly can.
So imagine a world where we are less connected to that model and our value is more aligned with the ability to serve our clients really well and help them solve problems.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McCormack and Leonard argue that generative AI is particularly consequential for legal work because law is language-based, uses relatively standardized documents, and has authoritative source material.
pts.d: McCormack describes an immediate impact for lawyers willing to experiment with the technology. Leonard identifies standardized legal writing and sources such as reporters, restatements, firms' internal documents, and courts' opinions as a combination with substantial potential. Their basis is an explanatory argument about the characteristics of legal work, rather than measured legal-task performance. Both explicitly disclaim being technologists. The claim concerns lawyers, legal professionals, firms, and courts, with organizational uses depending on appropriate data access and safeguards.

pts.k: Leonard predicts continued AI improvement and investment, while both speakers argue that lawyers can still catch up through participation and learning.
pts.d: Leonard rejects the idea that generative AI will simply disappear as a fad, citing the long history of AI research, technologists' career commitments, investment, and competition among major technology companies to integrate AI into existing products. These are reasons for her forecast, not a quantified growth or performance projection. McCormack attributes slow legal adoption partly to professional risk aversion; Leonard also points to workload and limited exposure to broader technology discussions. Their catch-up claim is situated in the early period of public generative-AI use, approximately a little over a year after November 2022. Leonard conditions her optimism on critical thought and safe deployment.

pts.k: The speakers describe organizational AI tools and commercially available legal-AI products as routes to operational learning and practice efficiency, including for smaller firms.
pts.d: Leonard describes building organizational tools on foundation models with confidentiality and security protections, internal data, testing, quality assessment, and benchmarking. McCormack reports that the AAA is using Microsoft products and training small tools to accelerate its own learning. She identifies vLex and CoCounsel as purchasable options for lawyers whose firms lack the capacity to develop their own tools. The AAA account is firsthand experience, but the episode supplies no quantified efficiency results. Smaller-firm efficiency is presented as a potential benefit, with possible client demands as an adoption driver; the speakers acknowledge uncertainty about CoCounsel's product integration.

pts.k: McCormack predicts that AI can improve courts' assistance to self-represented people and potentially strengthen public confidence in the justice system.
pts.d: McCormack calls the US civil justice system a market failure, stating that 92% of Americans cannot afford help navigating civil legal problems and that at least one party is unrepresented in 75% of civil cases in state courts. These figures are offered as context for unmet need, without a named study or data period. Her concrete example is a Maricopa County, Arizona court coordinator who has built custom GPT chatbots for self-represented parties. She presents these tools as relatively easy to build and capable of providing real help, but supplies no outcome study. Improved public confidence is explicitly conditional on courts and users obtaining better service and information. The affected groups are resource-constrained courts, judges, self-represented litigants, and the wider public.

pts.k: Leonard predicts pressure on hourly billing and associate leverage, rather than the complete disappearance of the billable hour.
pts.d: Leonard argues that faster task completion conflicts with revenue based on time worked and that increasingly capable AI will put pressure on revenue generated by junior associates' billable tasks. Leverage here concerns partners' use of associates to expand fee-earning capacity. She cites a recent Thomson Reuters report, tentatively identifying it as the Law Firm Financial Index, for a 20-year decline in hours billed per timekeeper across AmLaw 200 firms and practice areas, with rate increases offsetting that decline. This is historical business-model context, not evidence that AI caused the decline. The forecast is ongoing and conditional on AI becoming more capable; no displacement percentage, staffing shape, or deadline is specified. Partners, junior associates, and firm leaders are directly affected.

pts.k: Leonard predicts that corporate legal departments could retain overflow work using AI and redirect outside-counsel spending toward specialized advice.
pts.d: Leonard distinguishes work outsourced for expertise from work outsourced because the department lacks capacity. She argues that AI on the buyer side could absorb the latter, changing law firms' demand and revenue. This is a mechanism-based prediction, not a reported measurement of insourcing. It depends on in-house departments learning to use tools capable of handling work for which they already possess legal expertise. The timeframe is prospective and unspecified. General counsel, corporate leadership, in-house lawyers, and outside firms are affected; sophisticated specialist advice remains a reason to purchase external services.

pts.k: Leonard predicts that automation or alteration of junior work will disrupt apprenticeship-based lawyer development.
pts.d: Leonard argues that repetitive early-career tasks traditionally build judgment, strategy, and client-service skills. If AI removes or changes those tasks and compresses the associated developmental period, firms will need to reconsider junior responsibilities, talent-team support, and future leadership formation. Her basis is her characterization of the apprenticeship model and professional experience, with post-COVID skills disruption as additional context; no longitudinal training evidence is presented. This is a conditional forecast, not a finding that the apprenticeship period has already collapsed.

pts.k: McCormack predicts improved legal-department operations, spending forecasts, and resource allocation; Leonard reports a current strategy-development use.
pts.d: McCormack says businesses adopting AI elsewhere will expect their counsel's offices to achieve similar efficiencies. She predicts that departments can redesign legal-operations work, free resources for difficult questions requiring external expertise, and improve legal-spend planning. Her supporting experience is knowledge of unnamed general counsel departments using AI on billing to understand workflows. Leonard separately reports finding GPT-4 useful as a strategy thought partner, an augmentation use rather than autonomous legal advice. No quantified savings, forecasting accuracy, or strategy outcomes are supplied. McCormack also makes law-firm service redesign conditional on firms getting implementation right.

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack predict that AI-responsive law-school curricula could change recruitment patterns and reward innovative schools.
pts.d: Leonard argues that employers will need to examine schools' curricula for changing skills rather than assume educational uniformity. She identifies technology, design thinking, systems redesign, professionalism, and client focus as potential differentiators, mentioning Suffolk and Vanderbilt as programs she admires. McCormack predicts that schools using AI to improve education and teaching students about it could gain access to employers that previously recruited elsewhere. These are forecasts grounded in their legal-education experience, not placement data. McCormack specifies the coming years; success depends on substantive educational adaptation. Students, law-school programs, and recruiting firms are affected.

pts.k: The speakers predict personalized AI feedback and tutoring benefits for students; Leonard also forecasts competition for people able to teach emerging practice skills.
pts.d: Leonard proposes student-created custom GPTs using professors' sample exams, upper-class students' outlines, and hornbooks to support real-time self-testing. She anticipates learning, well-being, diversity, and inclusion benefits. McCormack emphasizes students reluctant to disclose confusion. Their basis is personal experience of law-school assessment and educational practice; McCormack refers generally to other disciplines, without naming research. These benefits are prospective, with no learning evaluation reported. Separately, Leonard predicts a talent crisis in finding people connected to current practice who can translate emerging skills into effective curricula, because firms will also value those skills. She says talent competition is already visible in firms but gives no examples or figures.

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack predict that widely available legal-information tools will challenge traditional unauthorized-practice regulation.
pts.d: Leonard anticipates difficult, recurring enforcement problems for state supreme courts while recognizing potential access-to-justice benefits. McCormack argues that people can create custom GPTs or obtain useful answers directly from ChatGPT, predicts improvement with successive models, and doubts that traditional regulatory approaches can keep pace. She advocates allowing experimentation that may help people with unmet legal needs, rather than claiming to have a complete regulatory solution. Her example is a reported New Jersey unauthorized-practice lawsuit against LegalZoom; she is uncertain whether she read it in Law360 or ALM. That example concerns regulatory activity, not an AI accuracy study or a judicial ruling establishing the legality of AI advice. The forecast affects regulators, public users, and providers of legal assistance, with no fixed deadline.

pts.k: Leonard envisages lawyer well-being benefits if AI helps firms reduce dependence on time-based revenue and focus more on client value.
pts.d: Leonard presents this as an optimistic possibility, not an observed outcome or a prediction that hourly billing will vanish. The proposed mechanism is loosening the connection between revenue and hours worked so that firms can emphasize solving client problems. It concerns experienced private-practice lawyers, firm leaders, and clients. No empirical evidence, implementation model, or date is supplied; the benefit depends on business-model change rather than AI capability alone.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The episode principally offers professional experience, illustrative examples, and mechanism-based forecasts, with limited quantitative context.
pts.d: The main numerical evidence is McCormack's uncited civil-justice need and representation figures and Leonard's account of a Thomson Reuters report on declining billable hours. Neither measures AI's effects. Concrete examples include Maricopa County chatbots, AAA experimentation, unnamed corporate billing uses, Leonard's GPT-4 strategy use, and a reported LegalZoom lawsuit. The speakers draw on careers in practice, courts, legal education, and ADR. No named legal-AI performance benchmark, measured hallucination rate, controlled learning study, quantified AI savings, or measured AI-driven employment change is presented. Leonard's reference to research tools hallucinating at an unspecified rate is not a numerical finding.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims combine early adoption observations in 2024 with largely undated, conditional forecasts; the show title does not establish a 2030 prediction deadline.
pts.d: Current observations concern experimentation, available products, some corporate billing applications, and court chatbots. Prospective changes depend on improving task capability, organizational adoption, safe deployment, revised service models, educational adaptation, and regulatory responses. The clearest explicit forward horizon is McCormack's expectation that educational innovators will be rewarded in the coming years. Leonard explicitly retains hourly billing within a future pricing portfolio. Both acknowledge uncertainty about the overall trajectory and the need to learn as events unfold.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The speakers distinguish impacts on providers, corporate buyers, education, courts, regulators, and people with unmet civil legal needs.
pts.d: For law firms, the predicted changes concern hourly revenue, associate leverage, junior development, recruitment, client relationships, and well-being; smaller firms are identified as buyers of ready-made products. For corporate legal departments and legal operations, the changes concern capacity, insourcing, workflow insight, spend forecasting, and purchasing specialist advice. For schools and students, they concern curricula, tutoring, recruitment opportunities, and competition for teaching talent. For courts, judges, and self-represented people, they concern affordable navigation assistance, better information, and public confidence. For state supreme courts and other regulators, they concern adapting unauthorized-practice oversight. The public access-to-justice claims are distinct from enterprise spending efficiencies.
